problem: Session 27 established that Ethernet frames are delivered locally using MAC addresses, but it left one big question unanswered: with hundreds of devices on an enterprise floor, how does a frame actually find the one correct destination out of a hundred wired ports, without simply repeating it out to everyone (which doesn't scale and leaks traffic to devices that shouldn't see it)? A hub-based network — where every frame is repeated out every port — collapses under its own traffic and offers zero isolation between devices.

Switching is the enterprise-scale answer: a device that intelligently learns where each MAC address lives and forwards frames only out the port that leads to the destination. Every modern wired enterprise network — from a 5- port office switch to a 96-port data center chassis — depends on switching to make local delivery fast, efficient, and reasonably contained.
concept: A switch is a Layer 2 (Data Link) device that connects multiple devices on the same network segment and forwards Ethernet frames based on destination MAC address, using a self-built MAC address table. Unlike a hub (pure electrical repeater, no intelligence), a switch inspects each frame and makes a per-port forwarding decision, giving each connected device effectively its own dedicated collision-free link (as covered in Session 27's duplex discussion).

Device OSI Layer Forwarding Decision Based On Scales To Hub Layer 1 None — repeats to all ports A handful of devices, poorly Switch Layer 2 Destination MAC address Hundreds of devices per switch, thousands per fabric Router Layer 3 Destination IP address Networks of networks (covered in Session 29)
deep: The MAC address table (CAM table) A switch builds its MAC address table (also called a CAM table, Content Addressable Memory table) dynamically by inspecting the source MAC address of every incoming frame and associating it with the port it arrived on. Entries typically age out after a period of inactivity (commonly 300 seconds by default on Cisco switches) to keep the table current as devices move or disconnect.
Learning — record the source MAC + incoming port for every frame seen.

Flooding — if the destination MAC isn't in the table yet, forward the frame out every port except the one it arrived on (this is safe because only the true owner will respond, and its reply will populate the table).
Forwarding/Filtering — once a destination MAC is known, send the frame out only that one port, and do not send it out any other port.

Switch types you'll encounter Type Description Unmanaged switch Plug-and-play, no configuration, no VLANs/monitoring — common in small offices/home use Managed switch (Layer 2) Configurable via CLI/GUI: VLANs, STP, port security, trunking — the enterprise standard Modular/chassis switch Data-center class, supports swappable line cards for high port density Broadcast domains All devices connected to a single switch (or set of switches without VLAN segmentation) share one broadcast domain — a broadcast frame (destination MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, e.g. an ARP request) is flooded to every device in it. This is a key limitation switching alone doesn't solve — VLANs (Session 33) exist specifically to split one physical switch into multiple logical broadcast domains.
4. Internal Workflow — A Frame's Journey Through a Switch Extending the Session 27 workflow, once a frame arrives at a switch port:
1. The switch reads the frame's source MAC and records/updates: (source MAC → ingress port) in its MAC address table.
2. The switch reads the frame's destination MAC and looks it up in the table.
3. If found: the switch forwards the frame out only the associated port (unicast forwarding) — every other port is unaffected, meaning other devices never even see this traffic.
4. If not found (or it's a broadcast/multicast address): the switch floods the frame out every port except the ingress port.
5. If the destination MAC is on the same port the frame arrived on, the switch drops it (filtering) — no need to send it back out the way it came.
This is exactly the mechanism briefly introduced in Session 27's "How switches use this frame" section — this session simply gives it full depth.
enterprise: In enterprise network design, switching typically happens in a layered architecture: access-layer switches connect end devices (PCs, phones, printers, APs); distribution-layer switches aggregate multiple access switches and often perform inter-VLAN routing; core-layer switches provide high-speed backbone connectivity between distribution blocks and to the WAN/data center. This three-tier (access/distribution/core) model is extremely common in CCNA material and real enterprise designs, and is worth memorizing as a mental map for where switching decisions happen at scale.

security: MAC flooding (introduced in Session 27) directly targets the CAM table described here — filling it with bogus entries forces the switch into fail-open flooding behavior, turning it into a de facto hub and enabling traffic interception.
Port security lets an administrator restrict how many (or which specific) MAC addresses are allowed on a given port, directly mitigating MAC flooding and unauthorized device connections.
VLAN hopping attacks exploit misconfigured trunk ports to send traffic into VLANs the attacker shouldn't have access to — a preview of the trunking concepts fully covered in Session 33.

Unused switch ports should be administratively disabled (shut down) or placed into an unused/quarantine VLAN — a simple but frequently-skipped hardening step, since an open live port is a free network entry point for anyone with physical access.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause Check Device can't reach anything, even same-subnet peers Port shut down, wrong VLAN, cable fault show interface status, show mac address-table Intermittent broadcast storms / network slowdown Switching loop (no STP or STP failure) show spanning-tree, check for redundant uncontrolled links Device sees traffic it shouldn't Port mirroring misconfigured, MAC flooding attack, hub inserted Review port config, check CAM table size/entries MAC address flapping between ports Loop, duplicate MAC, or misconfigured redundant link show mac address-table | look for same MAC on multiple ports Cisco IOS: show mac address-table | show interface status | show interface gi0/1 counters The MAC address table is your single most useful diagnostic tool at this layer — if a device can't be reached, checking whether its MAC even appears in the table (and on the expected port) usually narrows the problem within seconds.
example: Two PCs on the same floor suddenly can't reach each other, though both show "connected" locally. Checking the switch's MAC address table shows PC-A's MAC address flapping rapidly between two different ports — a strong signal of either a switching loop (someone plugged both ends of a cable into the same switch, or two switches into each other without STP) or a duplicate MAC address somewhere on the segment. Disconnecting the suspect cable resolves the flapping immediately, confirming an accidental loop was the cause. This is a textbook case where the CAM table itself — not any host-side tool — is what actually reveals the root cause, reinforcing why switch-side visibility matters even for what looks like a host problem.
cloud: Cloud environments replicate switching behavior entirely in software: a VPC/VNet's internal routing between instances in the same subnet is functionally MAC-learning-and-forwarding performed by the underlying software- defined network fabric, even though you never see a MAC address table directly. Container networking (Layer 8, Sessions 114-122) makes this even more visible — a Linux bridge or Open vSwitch instance on a container host builds and uses a MAC address table exactly as described in this session, just implemented as software rather than switch silicon.
automation: Switch administration is one of the most common places CLI automation gets applied in enterprise networking — pulling MAC address tables, interface statuses, and error counters across dozens of switches by hand doesn't scale.
This is a strong future pairing for your PowerShell/automation track once you move into network device automation (via SSH modules or vendor APIs, previewed in Session 108, REST APIs):
# Conceptual example once you reach network automation tooling:

# Connect via SSH to each switch, run 'show mac address-table', parse for anomalies (flapping MACs, oversized tables) Even without full network automation tooling yet, you can already script host-side switching diagnostics: `Get- NetNeighbor` (PowerShell) or `ip neigh` (Linux) show the local ARP/MAC neighbor cache, which is the host-side complement to a switch's MAC address table.
career: Switching fundamentals (MAC table behavior, flooding vs. forwarding, broadcast domains) are core CCNA exam content and among the most commonly asked practical questions in network/sysadmin interviews, precisely because they're easy to verify a candidate actually understands (rather than memorized) by asking a scenario question. Your Secure Branch Office lab already exercises these concepts hands-on — this session gives you the vocabulary to explain what you did there in interview-ready terms.

For Gulf-market IT roles, switch troubleshooting (interpreting MAC tables, interface counters, spotting loops) is a frequently under-taught but highly practical skill — being comfortable with it puts you ahead of candidates who only know switching in the abstract.

misconceptions: "A switch and a router do the same job." A switch forwards based on MAC addresses within one local segment; a router forwards based on IP addresses between different networks — they solve different problems at different layers, covered fully in the next session.

"More switch ports always means better performance." Port count doesn't matter if the switch's backplane/switching capacity can't handle all ports running at full speed simultaneously (oversubscription) — a spec worth checking on real hardware purchases.

"Flooding a frame to all ports is a bug or a security hole." It's normal, expected behavior for unknown destination MACs and is how the switch discovers where devices are — the actual security concern is when flooding happens because of a MAC table attack, not the mechanism itself.

"Switches remove the need for IP addressing." Switching only solves local delivery; without IP addressing and routing (Session 29+), devices on different subnets or different physical locations still couldn't communicate at all.
anchors: Three switch behaviors, in order: Learn (record source MAC), Flood (if destination unknown), Forward/Filter (if destination known) — "Learn, Flood, Forward."
"Hub = dumb repeater (Layer 1), Switch = smart local postman (Layer 2), Router = smart long-distance postman (Layer 3)."
CAM table = switch's memory of "who lives on which port" — built from source MACs, used to look up destination MACs.
A flapping MAC address in the table is almost always a loop or duplicate MAC — treat it as an immediate red flag.

lab: 1. Build a topology: 3 PCs connected to 1 switch. Before sending any traffic, check the switch's MAC address table (`show mac address-table`) and confirm it's empty.
2. Ping PC-A to PC-B. Immediately check the table again — confirm both MACs now appear, mapped to their correct ports.
3. In Simulation Mode, ping PC-A to PC-C and step through the flooding behavior on the very first frame (before PC-C's MAC is known) versus the unicast forwarding on the reply.

4. Deliberately create a loop: connect two ports of the same switch together with a cable (or connect two switches together twice). Observe what happens to traffic and the MAC table (in real hardware this causes a broadcast storm; Packet Tracer may throttle or warn) — this sets up Session 34 (STP), which exists to prevent exactly this.
5. Revisit your Secure Branch Office lab and check the MAC address table on each switch — identify which MACs you'd expect to see on which ports based on your topology.
notes: This session is a strong candidate for hands-on repetition rather than one pass — the Learn/Flood/Forward logic is simple to state but easy to gloss over without actually watching a MAC table build up in Simulation Mode. Worth spending extra Packet Tracer time here before moving to Session 29, since Routing assumes this local-delivery picture is already solid.

The loop exercise in the Lab section is deliberately a preview of pain — experiencing (even in simulation) why an uncontrolled loop is bad will make Session 34 (STP) land as "the fix for a problem I've seen" rather than an abstract protocol to memorize.
